bib.title: Building Applications with AI Agents, Chapter 5: Orchestration

question: How should an agent orchestrate tools and construct context for each model call to solve multistep tasks?
contributions: Three tool selection strategies compared (Table 5-2) with code
Tool topologies: single, parallel, chains, graphs

results.claim: Choose the simplest planning approach that meets the use case; start small and add complexity as needed.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
Choose the simplest planning approach that will meet your use case
requirements.

results.claim: Semantic tool selection is the most common pattern and is recommended for most use cases.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote: This is the most common pattern and is recommended for most use cases.

results.claim: Set a maximum length on tool chains because errors compound.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
It is highly recommended that a maximum
length be set to the tool chains, as errors can compound down the length
of the chain.

results.claim: Graphs cost more model calls and add cycle/unreachable/merge errors, so cap depth and branching factor and test routers.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
However, full graph execution typically incurs significantly more founda‐
tion model calls than chains—adding latency and cost—so it’s crucial to
cap depth and branching factor.

results.claim: Use a chain for strictly linear tasks; adopt a graph only when you must branch and later consolidate.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
Adopt a graph only
when you must both branch and later consolidate multiple streams of in‐
formation
results.note: Text is hyphen-broken in the PDF; line break may differ.

results.claim: Hierarchical tool selection is slower but often more accurate; not recommended unless there are many tools.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
While this is slower and would be expensive to parallelize, it reduces the
complexity of the tool selection task into two smaller chunks, and fre‐
quently results in higher overall tool selection accuracy.

results.claim: Standard tool selection adds a foundation-model call that can add seconds of latency.
results.setup: Book chapter guidance, no experiment; LangChain/LangGraph illustrative code
results.quote:
The main drawback is latency, as it requires another foundation
model call, which can add seconds to the overall response time.
results.note: Table 5-2 lists the con as poor scaling to many tools; the text names latency as the main drawback.

limits: No experiments or measurements; all trade-offs are qualitative.
Code listings are illustrative and partly broken (e.g. embed_text, graph.run(max_depth), handle_invoice routes to itself, get_stock_price undefined).
Author says the agent taxonomy is a starting point and evolving fast.
LangChain agent types and APIs (ZERO_SHOT_REACT_DESCRIPTION, LLMChain, ChatOpenAI gpt-4) have dated.
practices: Give each tool a concise descriptive name, a one-sentence summary, an example invocation and type/range constraints (Standard Tool Selection).
Use semantic tool selection for most cases; embed tool catalog once and embed the query with the same model (Semantic Tool Selection).
Use hierarchical selection only with a large number of semantically similar tools (Hierarchical Tool Selection).
Validate tool parameters with a basic parser and ask the model to correct failures; tune timeout and retry logic to latency needs (Tool Execution).
For parallel execution, retrieve a maximum number of tools (say five) semantically, then have the model filter to those needed (Parallel Tool Execution).
Cap chain length; prefer chains for linear tasks (Chains).
Sketch the graph on paper, cap depth/branching, unit-test each router, use tracing to check every path terminates (Graphs).
Context engineering: prioritise relevance, use structured formats such as MCP, summarise long histories, assemble context dynamically each step (Context Engineering).
Weigh latency vs accuracy, typical action count, how much plans must adapt, build test cases for planning approaches, choose simplest approach (Conclusion).

iteratively breaks a complex question into subquestions, invoking search per subquestion, then synthesizes (self-ask with search)
extends ReAct by reviewing past steps to identify and correct mistakes, grounding reasoning in goal-state reflections (ReflAct)
combines planner-executor, query decomposition and ReAct loops for open-ended investigations
index tool definitions with an embedding model and retrieve the most relevant tools by semantic search before the model chooses
organize tools into described groups; select a group, then search only within it
dynamically assembling all inputs (user messages, retrieved knowledge, workflow state, system prompts) into a structured, token-efficient context window
